name: Atlas Compute
heading: 3. Atlas Compute — Fort Pierce, 240 MW Planned
brief: Atlas Compute publicly describes a 240 MW AI-ready data-center campus in Florida, designed for high-density GPU computing. WFLX’s March 12 reporting ties its proposed site to Midway Industrial Park in the Fort Pierce area of St. Lucie County, where the company had secured land and a zoning-verification letter covered parcels around Post Office Road. The project was publicly discussed as a possible 2027 operation, not a guaranteed energization date. As of that March report, county staff said no formal project application had been submitted. The developer’s site confirms the 240 MW headline , but that does not independently certify a signed utility-service agreement, committed customer demand or operational IT capacity. A facility research profile updated October 20 still categorizes the project as proposed . Its location illustrates the power-interconnection and cooling challenges that accompany a large new AI site on Florida’s Atlantic coast.
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Florida (2026): Gigawatt Power, Water Permits and What Is Actually Approved

name: Cielo Digital Infrastructure
heading: 2. Cielo Digital Infrastructure — Haines City, 300 MW Target (Stalled)
brief: The 300 MW Cielo campus was identified near Marion Road and State Road 544 East in Haines City, Polk County. Data Center Dynamics’ July 17 investigation described a project on roughly 74 acres , seeking about 150,000 gallons of water per day . That daily water figure is a proposed demand, not documented actual consumption. Public officials interviewed by FOX 13 said the city lacked sufficient available permitted water capacity and had received no formal development agreement, site plan or zoning filing as of its June 25 report. A utility inquiry is not a construction authorization. The city sought a water-use permit modification through the Southwest Florida Water Management District, and regulators’ decision would not substitute for zoning and environmental reviews. Accordingly, Cielo stays second by its reported size , but the latest identifiable reporting describes its actual development status as stalled . A 300 MW marketing target must not be placed in an operating capacity total.
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Florida (2026): Gigawatt Power, Water Permits and What Is Actually Approved

name: Stonebridge / Fort Meade
heading: 1. Stonebridge / Fort Meade — 1,200 MW Proposed Electrical Load (Locally Approved)
brief: The largest substantially documented Florida proposal is Stonebridge’s planned campus on approximately 1,330 acres west of U.S. 98 in Fort Meade . In a June 15 public discussion, a Stonebridge principal described the scheme as 1.2 GW of power; the original recorded discussion is linked by Data Center Record . This is an announced campus electrical-load figure , not 1.2 GW of metered demand or a verified IT-only rating. The city’s commission voted unanimously on April 14 to approve a development agreement, following earlier land-use actions. That does not mean every construction and resource permit has been granted. The biggest obstacle was identified in a signed April 14 letter from the Southwest Florida Water Management District : the city’s then-current water-use permit did not cover the data center. District governing-board approval of a modified permit is required before regulated site activity. The same letter records a 2028 operational target, which is a plan , not a commissioning guarantee. name: QTS Blakely Campus
heading: 3. QTS Blakely Campus — 1,400 MW Potential Gross Capacity
brief: The proposed QTS campus in Blakely , Early County, is a rare example of a developer publishing a direct, full-scale energy figure while acknowledging how early the project remains. QTS’s own site states 1,400 MW of potential gross capacity for the concept. Gross infrastructure capacity can include mechanical systems and other overhead outside the servers themselves. It is not a contracted 1.4 GW IT workload, an approved delivery schedule or an operating load. QTS describes the facility as a concept-stage development with no fixed construction start date. Zoning, environmental review, design and utility agreements remain essential steps. The company says it intends to procure normal operating power from its utility, with emergency backup generators and a phased construction schedule potentially extending five to ten years. According to QTS, the developer would pay required energy-infrastructure costs. For local residents, the important outstanding information is the exact electric-service agreement, the approved site plan, the number of buildings and the projected cooling-water demand
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Georgia (2026): 3.2 GW OpenAI Campus, Bartow and Blakely Power Plans

name: Project Bunkhouse, Bartow County
heading: 2. Project Bunkhouse, Bartow County — 1,830 MW Early Site-Plan Demand
brief: The approximately 877-acre Project Bunkhouse site sits near Taff Road and Georgia Power’s Plant Bowen , northwest of Atlanta. An April 2025 Atlanta Journal-Constitution review of early plans reported 1,830 MW of possible power demand and three on-site substations. The initial state Development of Regional Impact filing, #4433 , described a campus approaching 8.7 million square feet and a possible investment of $19 billion at full buildout. In June 2025 , Bartow County’s sole commissioner approved the rezoning, with conditions and a final building-area cap of 8.3 million square feet . More recent official documentation gives a valuable correction: the county’s August 2026 policy statement calls Digital Realty’s Stilesboro investment approximately 1.3 GW of computing capacity , rather than 1.83 GW. These can describe different scopes—IT equipment versus overall site power—but the county document does not itself verify that a full 1.83 GW utility connection is approved. name: OpenAI Project Camellia, Effingham County
heading: 1. OpenAI Project Camellia, Effingham County — 3,200 MW Utility Agreement
brief: OpenAI’s Project Camellia , planned for the Savannah Gateway Industrial Hub in Effingham County, leads this ranking with an explicitly announced 3.2 GW electricity-service requirement . OpenAI says the power is expected in phases from 2028 through 2032 . Georgia Power confirmed in August 2026 that the regulatory process cleared its large-load agreement, including up to 1,000 MW of flexible demand response that could be curtailed during high grid demand. The July 22 Effingham County announcement describes at least $20 billion in private investment and an initial commitment to 400 long-term jobs . State regional-impact materials describe four major buildings and a peak electrical-load estimate near 3.21 GW, reflecting a slightly different modeling scope from the announced 3.2 GW agreement. OpenAI proposes closed-loop cooling to limit routine water consumption and has promised a community fund, education support and independent reporting. name: Servpac MTP Data Center
heading: 3. Servpac MTP Data Center — 1 MW Documented Available Power
brief: The Servpac MTP data center at 200 Kahelu Avenue in Mililani Technology Park occupies a 30,000-square-foot building designed for high-availability services. Its operator brochure reports 1 MW of available power , dual power distribution, backup generators, UPS equipment and redundant cooling. The facility earned Uptime Institute Tier IV Certification of Constructed Facility , reflecting its engineering focus on fault tolerance. A major new phase began in 2026. Servpac announced groundbreaking on January 22 for Building 2 , a $13 million expansion adding more than 15,500 square feet on five additional acres. The company said the project would more than double the center’s capacity and initially targeted completion during the second quarter. No updated full-campus MW rating or verified completion announcement was established in the records reviewed. The 1 MW figure above is therefore the original reported available power , not a newly commissioned campus total.

name: AlohaNAP, Kapolei
heading: 2. AlohaNAP, Kapolei — 2.7 MW Planned After Phase-One Expansion
brief: At 91-340 Farrington Highway in Kapolei , AlohaNAP provides a connection point for submarine-fiber routes, satellite traffic, regional carriers and cloud platforms. In October 2024, owners Harrison Street and 1547 Critical Systems Realty announced a 10,300-square-foot, 1.5 MW addition. Upon completion of the first phase, the complex was expected to have 22,800 square feet and 2.7 MW of total capacity . This is an announced development specification rather than confirmed energized computing capacity. AlohaNAP’s technical importance comes from connectivity as much as electricity. The owners describe access to five submarine-cable networks and more than 40 communication satellites , a valuable configuration for trans-Pacific communications. The site also supports AWS Direct Connect. Its older specification sheet identifies 1.5 MW of utility power for the original facility. A March 2026 operator tour still referred to a 1.5 MW expansion underway. The 2.7 MW project target should not be confused with the pre-expansion electrical service or a measured present-day IT load. articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Hawaii (2026)

name: DRFortress, Honolulu
heading: 1. DRFortress, Honolulu — 4.2 MW of Backup Power
brief: DRFortress , at 3375 Koapaka Street in Honolulu , is described by its operator as Hawaii’s largest carrier-neutral commercial data center. The 65,000-square-foot facility supports approximately 800 colocation cabinets as well as cloud services, private suites, interconnection and disaster recovery. Its current owner, 1547 Critical Systems Realty , publishes a 4.2 MW backup power specification with N+1 redundancy. Backup generator capacity is not an IT-load rating or a measure of current utility consumption , a key distinction when comparing DRFortress with other facilities. The Honolulu campus has developed through multiple expansion phases. In May 2023 , DRFortress announced completion of its fourth data center expansion, including 220 additional cabinets and a plan for two successive 500 kW additions in power density availability. Then in April 2025 , 1547 and Harrison Street announced they had acquired the business from GI Partners. Strong carrier connections, protective engineering and continuity services make the site a critical regional digital infrastructure hub.

name: Meta Kuna Data Center
heading: 3. Meta Kuna Data Center — 198 MW Estimated Operating Campus Capacity
brief: Meta announced on September 3, 2026 that its Kuna Data Center is officially online . The site near Kuna-Mora and Cole roads represents an investment of more than $1.2 billion and involved about 1,600 construction workers at peak . Meta’s formal opening statement confirms operating status but does not disclose a verified facility or IT megawatt rating . The company continues building at the site, including two rapid-deployment buildings documented by BoiseDev in October . Cleanview’s October 2026 data-center inventory estimates 99 MW for each of two operating Kuna buildings , or 198 MW for those structures combined. It is an independent capacity estimate, not the amount of power that Meta says it draws today. Epoch AI instead models 152 MW of IT power from imagery and cooling equipment; IT power and total facility power cannot be treated as equivalent. Meta also says it supported 645 MW of new renewable energy projects in Ada County . That number describes generation projects and is not the data center’s electricity demand.

name: Rhea Data Blacks Creek Campus
heading: 2. Rhea Data Blacks Creek Campus — 600 MW Preliminary Proposal
brief: The Rhea Data project, submitted by a subsidiary of Nevada-based Arevia Power, envisions a 600 MW data-processing complex south of Boise near Blacks Creek Reservoir and the Interstate 84 corridor . In September 2026, KIVI reported confirmation from the Bureau of Land Management of a roughly 4-million-square-foot , multi-building facility. The proposal involves about 3,700 acres of BLM-managed land across the broader project corridor and includes an on-site natural-gas power plant and electrical rights of way into Elmore County. Unlike the local zoning action for Gemstone, Rhea requires federal land-use processing, environmental review and public participation. The BLM confirmed the project was at the application stage as of September 21. Boise State Public Radio reported that the agency hoped to initiate the public scoping process before the end of 2026. That timeline is a forecast, not permission to build. The preliminary plan raises questions about water, the reservoir’s bird habitat, grid interconnection and fossil generation. name: Diode Ventures Gemstone Technology Park
heading: 1. Diode Ventures Gemstone Technology Park — 600–800 MW Full-Buildout Range
brief: Gemstone Technology Park is a 620-acre industrial data-center development at 3250 South Locust Grove Road near Barker Road in Kuna. A Diode Ventures representative told the April 2025 City Council hearing that the eventual campus might require 600–800 MW of electricity at full buildout , a range reported by the Idaho Statesman . The site is envisioned as a phased campus with several buildings, utility facilities and landscaped buffer areas. A reported investment above $1 billion is an anticipated development scale, not confirmed construction spending. In April 2025, the Kuna City Council approved Gemstone’s rezoning 3–2 , allowing the former agricultural property to be designated for light industrial development. That vote did not energize the proposed campus. Diode’s current project page still describes the development as early-stage, while a local-record tracker reports a legal challenge to its land-use approval. name: T5 Chicago IV, Grayslake
heading: 3. T5 Chicago IV, Grayslake — Approximately 1,550 MW Reported Grid Supply
brief: At Peterson and Alleghany roads in Grayslake, Lake County , T5 Data Centers’ Chicago IV is planned as a large phased hyperscale campus covering roughly 472–474 acres . The approved development envelope allows up to approximately 10 million square feet of floor area. Project reporting quotes 1.2 GW of potential IT load and roughly 1.55 GW of contracted ComEd electrical supply ; some sources round the secured service figure to 1.6 GW . The IT number describes capacity assigned to computing equipment, while the larger electrical figure also supports cooling, conversion and other site loads. Grayslake issued a permit for the first approximately 800,000-square-foot building on September 1, 2026 , with grading and utility work already visible. Initial delivery was projected for late 2027, not 2026. The village’s June FAQ estimates average daily water demand of no more than 50,000 gallons at full approved development, subject to how the buildings are actually configured. name: Project Cardinal, Yorkville
heading: 2. Project Cardinal, Yorkville — 1,800 MW Reported Planned Campus
brief: Project Cardinal , proposed by Pioneer Development, LLC , spans approximately 1,037 acres of farmland in Yorkville in Kendall County. The city’s application record describes 14 two-story data-center buildings totaling over 17 million square feet , two substations, a switchyard, seven stormwater basins and access roads. Independent project ledgers and contemporaneous filings report a planned 1.8 GW electrical scale; that is a development target rather than an amount approved for immediate delivery by ComEd. The proposed first building was targeted for 2029 in the developer’s application . The project’s approval is more complex than a single headline. Yorkville approved an annexation and planned-development framework , but parcel transfers, infrastructure commitments and additional phase implementation still matter. A June 2026 amendment request sought to extend a land-closing notice deadline from July 1, 2026 to December 31, 2027 , affecting approximately 305 acres of the original annexation. name: Joliet Technology Center
heading: 1. Joliet Technology Center — 1,800 MW Developer Buildout Estimate
brief: Joliet Technology Center is a planned 795-acre campus southwest of Chicago, near South Rowell Road and Bernhard Road , developed by Hillwood and PowerHouse Data Centers. The developer advertises a possible $20 billion investment , a phased campus of approximately 24 buildings and 1.8 GW of proposed full-buildout electrical demand . The city’s March 2026 legislative record independently documents the 1,800 MW developer projection, making this tied first-place entry documented directly as a reported planning figure . On March 19, 2026 , Joliet announced conditional approval of annexation for the property, with the associated rezoning and preliminary planned-development ordinances passed by City Council. The annexation depends on the developer completing acquisition. Individual future phases must still proceed through permits and final plans. A group of residents filed a lawsuit in May contesting approval procedures, according to local-record research . name: Project Beckham, Elkhart County
heading: 3. Project Beckham, Elkhart County — Approximately 1,500 MW Estimated, Tied
brief: Takanock’s Project Beckham is a proposed data-center development in Elkhart County near Goshen. In April 2025 testimony to Indiana utility regulators, Takanock founder Kenneth Davies described an estimated 1.5 GW data-center load and a dispute with Northern Indiana Public Service Company over the route and cost of electric service. Powered Lands’ project record summarizes the filing and identifies the proposal with Goshen. Davies said Takanock’s own modeling suggested that an existing 345-kilovolt transmission line could serve its request with limited network upgrades. That is a developer assessment, not proof of an approved interconnection or delivered power. An independently operated local information site describes the project as stalled and says its future is unclear; we could not independently confirm a current construction schedule. The 1,500 MW figure therefore represents an earlier estimated request, not an operating load or a guarantee that Beckham will proceed.

name: Digital Realty, Kokomo
heading: 2. Digital Realty, Kokomo — Approximately 1,500 MW Proposed, Tied
brief: Digital Realty’s Kokomo proposal calls for three buildings on approximately 476 acres at Industrial Park North. The company describes about 1 GW of IT capacity across roughly 3 million square feet. In October reporting on the proposal , a Digital Realty representative was quoted as estimating that the fully built campus would need about 1.5 GW of total facility power . This is a reported estimate, not a finalized utility interconnection agreement. The two numbers measure different things: IT capacity concerns computing equipment, while total facility demand also includes supporting systems. The city and developer have described a closed-loop, air-cooled system and a commitment to pay for necessary infrastructure. WISH-TV reported that Duke Energy was still working through electricity agreements and could not confirm whether upgrades would be needed. A full site plan had not been submitted at the time of that report. Kokomo’s mayor has discussed a 2033 completion target and projected tax revenue, but those outcomes depend on the project being developed and assessed.

name: Amazon Project Rainier, New Carlisle
heading: 1. Amazon Project Rainier, New Carlisle — Approximately 2,200 MW at Full Buildout
brief: Amazon Web Services’ New Carlisle campus in St. Joseph County is already partly operating and continues to expand. The published full-buildout figure is not a verified current utility draw. The South Bend Regional Chamber’s AWS environmental FAQ says the site is expected to use approximately 2.2 GW at completion . BitcoinVersus.Tech covered Amazon’s $11 billion Indiana announcement in 2024; the current campus is much further along than a land-only proposal. That 2.2 GW figure is the projected demand for the finished site, not a reading from its power meter today. Research group Epoch AI estimates about 1,037 MW of online IT power as of October 19, using satellite imagery and assumptions about commissioning. Its estimate is not an Amazon disclosure or a measurement of total site consumption.

name: COPT Defense, Van Meter
heading: 3. COPT Defense, Van Meter — Approximately 1,000 MW Estimated Capacity (Tied)
brief: COPT Defense Properties acquired a 365-acre parcel near Des Moines for $32 million in September 2024 to extend its data center shell-development business into Iowa. In its October 28, 2024 acquisition announcement , the company said the zoning could accommodate approximately 3.3 million square feet of future development with an estimated 1 GW of power capacity . That was a preliminary development figure, not a utility commitment to deliver 1 GW. COPT’s June 30, 2026 investor supplement still recorded a 365-acre, 3.3-million-square-foot land position under data center shell development. Industry tracking describes the site as a prospective long-term buildout constrained by electric service arrangements, with first buildings not confirmed to be under construction. The company specializes in developing powered building shells before tenants install their computing infrastructure. Consequently, the site’s land ownership and zoning are documented, while full electrical energization, occupancy and a completion date remain unverified.

name: Tract Altoona Technology Park
heading: 2. Tract Altoona Technology Park — 1,000 MW Advertised Site Capacity (Tied)
brief: Tract’s official Altoona project page lists 1,000 MW of capacity for its technology park, describes the property as owned and in development , and states it covers 468 acres . Tract originally announced acquisition of 453 fully entitled acres in September 2025 , describing a 1 GW-plus opportunity on an existing 345 kV transmission corridor . The two published acreage numbers reflect different dated descriptions; the current project page’s 468-acre figure is used here instead of silently treating them as identical. Tract’s project materials state the land has data-center zoning and a development agreement supported by utility studies. They also list a 588,000-gallon-per-day water reservation ; that is a reservation or planning allowance, not measured daily consumption . The developer’s business is to prepare and position large sites for future hyperscale customers. A 1,000 MW site capability claim does not establish executed tenant leases, interconnected power at that scale, or delivery of operating computing capacity. name: QTS Cedar Rapids
heading: 1. QTS Cedar Rapids — Approximately 1,050–1,133 MW Reported Planned Scale
brief: QTS Data Centers’ August 8, 2025 announcement describes a seven-building campus on 612 acres at the Big Cedar Industrial Center in southwest Cedar Rapids. The Blackstone-backed company projected up to $10 billion of long-term investment . The developer and utility confirm that construction is occurring, unlike the mostly land-stage projects at Altoona and Van Meter. QTS does not disclose a single definitive full-campus MW rating in that announcement. The Business Record’s September 2026 review describes the QTS development as requiring about 1.05 GW . An Iowa clean-energy district resource inventory separately lists 616 MW in a first phase and 517 MW in a second , adding to 1,133 MW . name: Red Wolf DCD Properties, Kansas City
heading: 3. Red Wolf DCD Properties, Kansas City — 600 MW Proposed
brief: The Red Wolf proposal would occupy land on both sides of Parallel Parkway near Kansas Speedway in western Wyandotte County. KCUR’s January 29, 2026 investigation , based on local utility and government proceedings, describes a roughly 548-acre development with a proposed 600 MW electrical requirement—approximately 300 MW north and 300 MW south of the parkway. The broader concept includes multiple data center buildings, major electrical substations and connecting infrastructure. Development status is less settled than the size suggests. The local-record chronology documents a south-tract zoning approval , but also describes a failed supermajority vote on the northern tract following a protest petition. Residents challenged the zoning process in court. As of the January 2026 reporting, no final signed deal existed with the Board of Public Utilities (BPU) or Unified Government. That is not equivalent to approval of the whole 600 MW campus or commencement of construction. The updated plan covers more than 1,000 acres near the Tonganoxie/Eudora I-70 interchange, according to KCTV’s contemporaneous reporting and local project tracking. The developer says it will fund incremental transmission and generation upgrades associated with the development, rather than pass those new costs to existing customers. name: Digital Realty, Astra Enterprise Park, De Soto
heading: 1. Digital Realty, Astra Enterprise Park, De Soto — 2,000 MW Eventual Utility Service
brief: Digital Realty’s June 22, 2026 investor announcement is the strongest capacity evidence in this Kansas ranking. The company said it acquired approximately 1,440 acres at Astra Enterprise Park , on the former Sunflower Army Ammunition Plant property in De Soto, in a transaction valued at approximately $475 million . It disclosed an Energy Service Agreement to provide 600 MW of utility power by early 2028 , rising to 2 GW at full delivery . The latter figure is a future contractual development objective, not data center energy consumption today. The City of De Soto’s project portal describes the initial Astra North phase as roughly 280 acres , with up to nine buildings totaling around 3 million square feet . Astra North is only part of the much larger landholding, which also includes Astra South. It would be inaccurate to say the nine proposed North buildings are already using the entire 2 GW development allocation.
